decks.title: Logarithms — Part 1: Two forms, valid values and common logarithms
goals: Write a power as a logarithm and a logarithm as a power
Say which bases and numbers are allowed, and use log of one is zero and log of the base is one
Evaluate simple logarithms, including common logarithms to base ten
Find an unknown base or number by converting to exponential form

slides.heading: Logarithms, Part 1
slides.body_md: A logarithm answers one question: **to what power must the base be raised to give this number?**

visual.alt: Flow with two boxes: a to the x equals N, and log base a of N equals x. An arrow labelled write as a logarithm goes from the first to the second, and an arrow labelled write as a power goes back.
visual.caption: Two ways of saying the same fact.

slides.narration: Welcome to logarithms. A logarithm answers one question: to what power must the base be raised to give this number? Every logarithm is just a power written the other way round. In this part we learn the two forms, which values are allowed, the special values, and common logarithms to base ten.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Know which **bases and numbers** are allowed
Find an unknown base or number
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First we convert between powers and logarithms. Then we see which bases and numbers are allowed, and the two special values. Finally we meet common logarithms, which use base ten, and we find unknown bases and numbers.

slides.heading: Two forms of one fact
slides.body_md: $a^{x} = N$ and $\log_{a} N = x$ say exactly the same thing. The logarithm **is** the exponent.

visual.alt: Table with six facts, each written as a power and as a logarithm. Two to the five is thirty two, so log base two of thirty two is five. Ten cubed is one thousand. Five to the minus two is one twenty fifth. Nine to the half is three. Sixteen to the three quarters is eight. One half to the fourth is one sixteenth.
visual.caption: The base stays the base, the exponent becomes the logarithm, and the result of the power becomes the number.

slides.narration: Look at the table. Two to the power five is thirty two, so the logarithm of thirty two to base two is five. Ten cubed is one thousand, so the logarithm of one thousand to base ten is three. Notice that the logarithm can be a negative number or a fraction, as in the last four rows. The base stays the base, and the exponent becomes the logarithm.

slides.heading: Base, number and logarithm
slides.body_md: In $\log_{a} N = x$ the three parts have different jobs and different conditions.

visual.alt: Table naming the parts of log base a of N equals x. The base a must be positive and not one. The number N must be positive. The logarithm x can be any real number. Example: log base two of eight equals three, with base two, number eight and logarithm three, because two cubed is eight.
visual.caption: In $\log_{a} N = x$ the base is $a$, the number is $N$ and the logarithm is $x$.

slides.narration: In a logarithm statement, a is the base, N is the number, and x is the logarithm. The base must be positive and not equal to one, and the number must be positive. The logarithm itself can be any real number. For example, the logarithm of eight to base two is three, because two cubed is eight.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a power as a logarithm
slides.body_md: Which line says the same as $4^{3} = 64$?
slides.narration: Find the base, the exponent and the number in the power. Then decide which line has the same base, puts the number after it, and equals the exponent.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from powers to logarithms
slides.body_md: Write each fact in logarithmic form.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Name the base $a$, the exponent $x$ and the number $N$.
**Answer —** see the table: for example $8^{\frac{2}{3}} = 4$ becomes $\log_{8} 4 = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

visual.alt: Table with four statements changed from exponential to logarithmic form. Three to the fourth is eighty one. Seven to the minus one is one seventh. Eight to the two thirds is four. Ten to the minus three is zero point zero zero one. Each shows base, exponent, number and the logarithmic form.
visual.caption: Identify the base, the exponent and the number, then write $\log_{a} N = x$.

slides.narration: For each fact, name the base, the exponent and the number, then write log of the number to that base equals the exponent. Three to the fourth is eighty one gives log of eighty one to base three equals four. Eight to the two thirds is four gives log of four to base eight equals two thirds. And ten to the minus three is zero point zero zero one gives log of zero point zero zero one to base ten equals minus three.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: evaluating a logarithm
slides.body_md: Find $\log_{8} 32$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** Write both sides as powers of $2$: $2^{3x} = 2^{5}$.

visual.alt: Table of five steps finding log base eight of thirty two. Call it x, write eight to the x equals thirty two, rewrite both sides as powers of two so that two to the three x equals two to the five, equate exponents to get x equals five thirds, and check that eight to the five thirds is thirty two.
visual.caption: Write both sides as powers of one base, then compare exponents.

slides.narration: To evaluate a logarithm, call it x and convert to a power. Eight to the x equals thirty two. Neither number is a power of the other, but both are powers of two. So two to the three x equals two to the five. Equal powers of the same base have equal exponents, so three x is five and x is five thirds.

slides.heading: Why these conditions?
slides.body_md: The restrictions are not arbitrary: without them the definition breaks down.

visual.alt: Table of three restrictions. A base of one is useless because one to any power is one. A negative base such as minus two has no real value for minus two to the half. A number that is zero or negative can never equal a positive base raised to a power.
visual.caption: A logarithm needs $a > 0$, $a \ne 1$ and $N > 0$.

slides.narration: Why must the base be positive and not one? If the base were one, every power of it is one, so the logarithm of eight would have no value, and the logarithm of one would have every value. A negative base has no real value for a half power. And a positive base raised to any power stays positive, so zero and negative numbers have no logarithm at all.

slides.heading: Two special values
slides.body_md: $\log_{a} 1 = 0$ because $a^{0} = 1$, and $\log_{a} a = 1$ because $a^{1} = a$. More generally $\log_{a} a^{x} = x$.

visual.alt: Table for five bases: two, five, ten, thirteen and one half. For every base the logarithm of one is zero, the logarithm of the base itself is one, and the logarithm of the base cubed is three.
visual.caption: Whatever the base: $\log_{a} 1 = 0$, $\log_{a} a = 1$, $\log_{a} a^{x} = x$.

slides.narration: Two values hold for every base. The logarithm of one is zero, because any base to the power zero is one. The logarithm of the base itself is one, because a base to the power one is the base. And more generally, the logarithm of a to the x, to base a, is just x. The table shows these for five different bases.

slides.heading: Quick check: which has no value?
slides.body_md: Think about what a positive base can produce.
slides.narration: Turn each expression into a power equation. Ask whether any power of a positive base could ever equal that number.

slides.heading: Common logarithms
slides.body_md: When no base is written, the base is $10$: $\log N$ means $\log_{10} N$. Powers of ten give whole-number logarithms.

visual.alt: Table of common logarithms. The log of zero point zero zero one is minus three, of zero point zero one is minus two, of zero point one is minus one, of one is zero, of ten is one, of one hundred is two, and of one thousand is three.
visual.caption: The common logarithm uses base $10$ and is written $\log N$.

slides.narration: Logarithms to base ten are called common logarithms, and the base is usually left out. The table shows that the logarithm of a power of ten is just its exponent. A thousand is ten cubed, so its logarithm is three. And a thousandth is ten to the minus three, so its logarithm is minus three. Numbers between powers of ten have logarithms between whole numbers.

slides.heading: The graph of log x
slides.body_md: The curve $y = \log x$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 1$, rises slowly, and exists **only for $x > 0$**.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals log of x to base ten for x from zero point zero five to twenty. The curve rises slowly from the left, crosses the x axis at x equals one, and passes through the points zero point one, minus one and ten, one. It exists only for positive x.
visual.caption: The graph of $y = \log x$ lies to the right of the $y$-axis: only positive numbers have logarithms.

slides.narration: This is the graph of the common logarithm. It crosses the horizontal axis at one, because the logarithm of one is zero. It passes through ten, one, and through zero point one, minus one. It rises very slowly, and it only exists to the right of the vertical axis, since only positive numbers have logarithms.

slides.heading: Quick check: a small concentration
slides.body_md: Write the number as a power of ten.
slides.narration: Write the decimal as one over a power of ten, then as ten to a negative power. The exponent is the common logarithm.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding the base
slides.body_md: Find $x$ if $\log_{x} \dfrac{1}{81} = -4$.

visual.alt: Table of four steps to find the base x when log base x of one eighty first is minus four. Write x to the minus four equals one eighty first, so x to the fourth is eighty one, so x is three, because a base is positive. Check that three to the minus four is one eighty first.
visual.caption: A base is always positive, so reject $x = -3$.

slides.narration: To find an unknown base, convert to a power. The base to the minus four equals one eighty first. Take reciprocals: the base to the fourth equals eighty one. The fourth root of eighty one is three. We reject minus three, because a base must be positive. And three to the minus four is indeed one eighty first.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: finding the number
slides.body_md: Find $x$ if $\log_{4} x = \dfrac{5}{2}$.

visual.alt: Table of four steps to find x when log base four of x is five halves. Then x is four to the five halves. The square root of four is two, so x is two to the fifth, which is thirty two. Check that log base four of thirty two is five halves.
visual.caption: Take the root named by the denominator, then the power named by the numerator.

slides.narration: To find an unknown number, convert to a power and calculate. The number is four to the power five halves. The denominator two asks for a square root, which is two. The numerator five asks for the fifth power of that, which is thirty two. So the number is thirty two, and the check agrees.

slides.heading: Moving the decimal point
slides.body_md: In exercises, $\log 7 = 0.8451$ may be **given**. Then $\log 70$, $\log 700$ and $\log 0.07$ follow from $\log 10 = 1$.

visual.alt: Table of five numbers built from seven. Given log seven is zero point eight four five one, log seventy is one point eight four five one, log seven hundred is two point eight four five one, log zero point seven is minus zero point one five four nine and log zero point zero seven is minus one point one five four nine.
visual.caption: Moving the decimal point changes $\log$ by a whole number, because $\log 10 = 1$.

slides.narration: Suppose the logarithm of seven is given as zero point eight four five one. Seventy is seven times ten, so add one to get one point eight four five one. Seven hundred adds two. Zero point seven is seven divided by ten, so subtract one. In examinations the needed values are given, so log tables are not required.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: an acidity score
slides.body_md: An imagined score is $-\log c$. Find it for $c = 5 \times 10^{-4}$, given $\log 5 = 0.6990$.

visual.alt: Table of four steps for an acidity score defined as minus log c, with c equal to five times ten to the minus four and log five equal to zero point six nine nine zero. Log c is log five minus four, which is minus three point three zero one, so the score is three point three zero one.
visual.caption: The score $-\log c$ is positive for small concentrations.

slides.narration: A score is defined as minus the common logarithm of a concentration. Here the concentration is five times ten to the minus four. Its logarithm is the logarithm of five plus the logarithm of ten to the minus four, which is zero point six nine nine zero minus four, or minus three point three zero one. So the score is three point three zero one.

slides.heading: Quick check: a valid base
slides.body_md: Decide whether this statement is correct.
slides.narration: Recall what the definition requires of a base. Then ask whether a negative number meets those requirements.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $\log N$ with no base means base $10$
Unknown base or number: convert to a power and match bases

rows: convert to exponential form, then match bases

visual.alt: Summary table of part one. Powers and logarithms are two forms of one fact. The base is positive and not one and the number is positive. Log of one is zero and log of the base is one. A common logarithm has base ten. Convert to exponential form to find unknowns.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. A power and a logarithm are two forms of one fact. The base is positive and not one, and the number is positive. The logarithm of one is zero and the logarithm of the base is one. A logarithm with no base written has base ten. To find unknowns, convert to a power and match bases.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Conversion (1 mark each):** base, exponent and number in the right places
**Unknown base:** exponential form 1 + solve 1 + reject a negative base 1
**Mistake:** writing $\log_{a} N = x$ with $N$ and $x$ swapped
**Mistake:** forgetting that the base must be positive
**Mistake:** writing a negative logarithm as a negative number: $\log 0.001 = -3$, but $0.001$ is positive
slides.narration: In conversions, check the base, the exponent and the number are in the right places. When finding an unknown base, give the exponential form, solve, and reject any negative base. Do not mix up the two special values: the logarithm of one is zero, and the logarithm of the base is one. And remember that a logarithm can be negative, but the number cannot.

decks.title: Logarithms — Part 2: The laws, expanding and simplifying, and equations
goals: State and use the product, quotient and power laws
Expand an expression into logarithms of its factors and combine logarithms into one
Write logarithms in terms of log 2, log 3 and log 5 and use given values
Solve simple logarithm equations with a domain check and prove simple identities

slides.heading: Logarithms, Part 2
slides.body_md: Three laws turn **products into sums**, **quotients into differences** and **powers into multipliers**.

visual.alt: Flow with a heading, the laws of logarithms, and three boxes below it: the product law, the quotient law and the power law, each written in symbols.
visual.caption: Three laws, one base.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Logarithms are useful because of three laws. A logarithm turns a product into a sum, a quotient into a difference, and a power into a multiplier. In this part we prove and use these laws, expand and combine expressions, use given values, solve equations and prove identities.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: State and use the **product, quotient and power laws**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We learn the three laws and why they hold. We expand an expression into separate logarithms and combine separate logarithms into one. We use given values, solve equations while checking the domain, and prove simple identities.

slides.heading: The product law
slides.body_md: $\log_{a}(mn) = \log_{a} m + \log_{a} n$ for positive $m$ and $n$. The base must be the same on both sides.

visual.alt: Table of four products using given values of logarithms. Log two plus log three is zero point seven seven eight one, the logarithm of six. Log three plus log seven is one point three two two two, the logarithm of twenty one. Log two plus log five is exactly one, the logarithm of ten. Log five plus log seven is one point five four four one, the logarithm of thirty five.
visual.caption: Adding logarithms corresponds to multiplying numbers: $\log m + \log n = \log mn$.

slides.narration: The product law says the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms. Look at the table. The logarithm of two plus the logarithm of three gives the logarithm of six. The logarithm of two plus the logarithm of five is exactly one, which is the logarithm of ten. The sum is easier to handle than the product, which is why logarithms were invented.

slides.heading: Why the product law holds
slides.body_md: It is the law of indices $a^{x} \times a^{y} = a^{x+y}$ written in logarithmic form.

nodes.label: Let $\log_{a} m = x$ and $\log_{a} n = y$

visual.alt: Flow chart proving the product law: let the logs of m and n be x and y; then m is a to the x and n is a to the y; their product is a to the x plus y; so the log of m n is x plus y; so the log of the product is the sum of the logs.
visual.caption: The product law is the law of indices $a^{x} a^{y} = a^{x + y}$ read backwards.

slides.narration: Here is the proof. Let the logarithm of m be x and the logarithm of n be y. Then m is a to the x and n is a to the y. Multiplying, m n is a to the x plus y, because we add indices when we multiply powers. Writing that as a logarithm, the logarithm of m n is x plus y, which is the sum of the two logarithms.

slides.heading: The quotient law
slides.body_md: $\log_{a}\dfrac{m}{n} = \log_{a} m - \log_{a} n$. It comes from $\dfrac{a^{x}}{a^{y}} = a^{x-y}$.

visual.alt: Table of four differences. Log one thousand minus log ten is log one hundred, which is two. Log base two of ninety six minus log base two of three is log base two of thirty two, which is five. Log base three of fifty four minus log base three of two is log base three of twenty seven, which is three. Log seven minus log seventy is log of one tenth, which is minus one.
visual.caption: Subtracting logarithms corresponds to dividing numbers: $\log \dfrac{m}{n} = \log m - \log n$.

slides.narration: The quotient law says the logarithm of a quotient is the difference of the logarithms. The logarithm of a thousand minus the logarithm of ten is the logarithm of a hundred, which is two. It works in any base, as the second and third rows show. And the logarithm of seven minus the logarithm of seventy is the logarithm of one tenth, which is minus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: recognising the product law
slides.body_md: Which line is correct for every positive $m$ and $n$?
slides.narration: Test each line with small numbers such as two and three. Only one of the lines is true every time.

slides.heading: The power law
slides.body_md: $\log_{a} m^{p} = p\log_{a} m$. In particular $\log_{a} a^{x} = x$.

visual.alt: Table of four power-law examples. Log thirty two is five log two, which is one point five zero five. Log of one eighth is minus three log two, which is minus zero point nine zero three. Log of the square root of ten is one half of log ten, which is one half. Log base five of five to the seven is seven times log base five of five, which is seven.
visual.caption: The power becomes a multiplier: $\log m^{p} = p\log m$, and so $\log_{a} a^{x} = x$.

slides.narration: The power law says the logarithm of a power is the exponent times the logarithm. So the logarithm of thirty two is five times the logarithm of two. A fraction like one eighth is two to the minus three, giving minus three times the logarithm of two. A square root is a power of one half. And the logarithm of five to the seven, to base five, is simply seven.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: combining with the product law
slides.body_md: Simplify $\log 8 + \log 125$.

visual.alt: Table of three steps simplifying log eight plus log one hundred twenty five. The product law gives log of eight times one hundred twenty five, which is log one thousand, which equals three.
visual.caption: Spot a product that makes a power of $10$.

slides.narration: Add the two logarithms by multiplying the numbers. Eight times one hundred twenty five is one thousand, a power of ten. The logarithm of one thousand is three. Whenever you add logarithms, look for factors that multiply to a power of the base, such as ten, one hundred or one thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: power law then product law
slides.body_md: Write $2\log 5 + 3\log 2$ as a single logarithm.

visual.alt: Table of three steps writing two log five plus three log two as one logarithm. Use the power law to get log twenty five plus log eight, then the product law to get log two hundred.
visual.caption: Power law first, then product or quotient law.

slides.narration: When there are multipliers in front of the logarithms, use the power law first. Two log five becomes the logarithm of twenty five, and three log two becomes the logarithm of eight. Then the product law gives the logarithm of twenty five times eight, which is two hundred. Always move the multipliers inside before combining.

slides.heading: Quick check: a cancelling pair
slides.body_md: Move each multiplier inside its logarithm first.
slides.narration: Use the power law to write each term as a single logarithm. Compare the two numbers you get, and decide what their difference is.

slides.heading: Expanding an expression
slides.body_md: To **expand**, split products and quotients, then bring powers down. A root is a power: $\sqrt{x} = x^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

visual.alt: Table of five expressions and their expansions. Log of a b is log a plus log b. Log of a over b is log a minus log b. Log of x cubed y squared over z is three log x plus two log y minus log z. Log of the square root of x over y is half log x minus half log y. Log of one over x to the fourth is minus four log x.
visual.caption: Product and quotient laws split the expression; the power law brings the powers down.

slides.narration: Expanding means writing one logarithm as a sum of simple logarithms. Split products into sums, quotients into differences, and bring the powers down. A square root counts as a power of one half. A reciprocal, such as one over x to the fourth, gives a minus sign and so the logarithm is minus four log x.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: expanding with four letters
slides.body_md: Expand $\log \dfrac{a^{3}\sqrt{b}}{c^{2} d}$.

visual.alt: Table of three steps expanding log of a cubed root b over c squared d. Split into log of the top minus log of the bottom, use the product law on each, then the power law, and remove the bracket carefully so that both log c squared and log d are subtracted.
visual.caption: The minus sign in front of the bracket applies to both terms inside.

slides.narration: First split the top from the bottom with the quotient law. Then split each product with the product law. The bottom is inside a bracket after a minus sign. Finally the power law brings down the three, the half and the two. When the bracket is removed, both the log of c squared and the log of d are subtracted.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the right expansion
slides.body_md: Apply the three laws one at a time.
slides.narration: Split the fraction first, then the product on top, then bring down the powers. Be careful with the sign of the term from the bottom.

slides.heading: In terms of log 2, log 3, log 5
slides.body_md: Factorise the number into $2$, $3$, $5$. Use $\log 10 = 1$: for example $\log 5 = \log \dfrac{10}{2} = 1 - \log 2$.

visual.alt: Table of five numbers written using the logarithms of two, three and five, with log ten equal to one. Twelve is two log two plus log three, one point zero seven nine one. Fifteen is log three plus log five, one point one seven six one. Eighteen is log two plus two log three, one point two five five two. Five is one minus log two, zero point six nine nine. Zero point three is log three minus one, minus zero point five two two nine.
visual.caption: Factorise into $2$, $3$, $5$ (and $10$); the laws do the rest.

slides.narration: A very common task is to write a logarithm using only the logarithms of two, three and five. Factorise the number. Twelve is two squared times three. Eighteen is two times three squared. And five is ten divided by two, so its logarithm is one minus the logarithm of two. Zero point three is three tenths, so we subtract one.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: using given values
slides.body_md: Given $\log 2 = 0.3010$ and $\log 3 = 0.4771$, find $\log 54$.

visual.alt: Table of four steps finding log fifty four from the given log two equal to zero point three zero one zero and log three equal to zero point four seven seven one. Fifty four is two times three cubed, so log fifty four is log two plus three log three, which is zero point three zero one zero plus one point four three one three, one point seven three two three.
visual.caption: Always factorise into the primes whose logarithms are given.

slides.narration: When values are given, factorise into the numbers whose logarithms you know. Fifty four is two times twenty seven, and twenty seven is three cubed. So the logarithm is the logarithm of two plus three times the logarithm of three. Three times zero point four seven seven one is one point four three one three, and adding zero point three zero one zero gives one point seven three two three.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a logarithm equation

visual.alt: Table of five steps solving log base two of x plus log base two of x minus two equals three. The product law gives x times x minus two equals eight, so x squared minus two x minus eight is zero, so x is four or minus two. Both logarithms need x greater than two, so reject minus two and keep four. Check: two plus one is three.
visual.caption: Always test each root against the domain.

slides.narration: Combine the two logarithms with the product law, then convert to a power. The product x times x minus two equals two cubed, which is eight. That is a quadratic with roots four and minus two. But both logarithms need x to be greater than two, so minus two is rejected. The only solution is four, and the check gives two plus one equals three.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a single logarithm

visual.alt: Table of three steps solving log base four of three x minus five equals two. Write three x minus five equals sixteen, so x is seven. Check the domain: three times seven minus five is sixteen, which is positive.
visual.caption: Convert at once when there is a single logarithm.

slides.narration: With a single logarithm, convert at once. Three x minus five equals four squared, which is sixteen. So three x is twenty one and x is seven. Always finish with the domain check: when x is seven, the argument is sixteen, which is positive, so the solution is valid.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: proving an identity
slides.body_md: Show that $\log 48 - \log 3 = 4\log 2$.

visual.alt: Table of three steps proving log forty eight minus log three equals four log two. By the quotient law the left side is log of forty eight over three, which is log sixteen, and since sixteen is two to the fourth, this equals four log two.
visual.caption: Start from the more complicated side and work towards the other.

slides.narration: To prove an identity, start from the more complicated side. The quotient law turns the difference into the logarithm of forty eight over three, which is sixteen. Sixteen is two to the fourth, so the power law gives four times the logarithm of two. That is exactly the right side, so the identity is proved.

slides.heading: Quick check: a quotient equation
slides.body_md: Combine, convert, solve, then check the domain.
slides.narration: Use the quotient law to make one logarithm, convert to a power, and solve the resulting equation. Finally test that every argument is positive.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Equations: combine, convert, solve, **check the domain**

rows: combine, convert, solve, then check the domain

visual.alt: Summary table of part two: the product, quotient and power laws; solving equations by combining, converting, solving and checking the domain; and a warning that the log of a sum is not the sum of the logs.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. The product law adds, the quotient law subtracts, and the power law multiplies. To solve an equation, combine the logarithms, convert to a power, solve, and always check the domain. And remember: the logarithm of a sum is not the sum of the logarithms.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Expand or combine (2 marks):** law used 1 + result 1
**Equation (3 marks):** combine and convert 1 + solve 1 + domain check 1
**Mistake:** keeping a root that makes an argument negative, or losing the minus sign on a term from a bracket
slides.narration: In expansion questions, name the law you are using. For given values, show the factorisation first. In equations, you must check the domain, because a root that makes an argument negative has to be rejected. Never write that the logarithm of a sum is the sum of the logarithms, and never turn a quotient of logarithms into a difference.

notes.title: Logarithms — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Exponential form and logarithmic form
sections.body_md:
A **logarithm** is an exponent. The two statements $a^{x} = N$ and $\log_{a} N = x$ say the same thing, with $a > 0$, $a \ne 1$ and $N > 0$.

- In $\log_{a} N = x$: $a$ is the **base**, $N$ the **number** (argument) and $x$ the **logarithm**.
- To convert, keep the base, turn the exponent into the logarithm, and put the result of the power after the base: $8^{\frac{2}{3}} = 4 \iff \log_{8} 4 = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
- To evaluate $\log_{8} 32$, put $x = \log_{8} 32$, write $8^{x} = 32$, rewrite both sides as powers of $2$, and equate the exponents: $2^{3x} = 2^{5}$, so $x = \dfrac{5}{3}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The exponent to which the base must be raised to give the number: $\log_{a} N = x$ means $a^{x} = N$.
The number $N > 0$ whose logarithm is taken.

sections.heading: 2. Valid bases and numbers; two special values
sections.body_md:
A base must be positive and not $1$: if $a = 1$ every power is $1$, and a negative base has no real value for a power such as $\frac{1}{2}$. A number must be positive, because a positive base raised to any power is positive: $\log_{5} 0$ and $\log_{5}(-25)$ do not exist. A logarithm itself can be negative or a fraction.

- $\log_{a} 1 = 0$ because $a^{0} = 1$.
- $\log_{a} a = 1$ because $a^{1} = a$; more generally $\log_{a} a^{x} = x$.
- The graph of $y = \log x$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 1$ and lies to the right of the $y$-axis.

sections.heading: 3. Common logarithms and given values
sections.body_md:
When no base is written the base is $10$: $\log N$ means $\log_{10} N$. A power of ten has a whole-number logarithm: $\log 0.001 = -3$, $\log 1000 = 3$. Because $\log 10 = 1$, moving the decimal point changes the logarithm by a whole number: if $\log 7 = 0.8451$ then $\log 70 = 1.8451$ and $\log 0.07 = -1.1549$.

In problems the needed values (for example $\log 2 = 0.3010$, $\log 3 = 0.4771$) are **given**; log tables and antilog tables are not required.

**Number of digits:** if $\log N = k + f$ with $k$ a whole number and $0 \le f < 1$, then $N$ has $k + 1$ digits. For $2^{40}$: $40 \times 0.3010 = 12.04$, so $13$ digits.

sections.heading: 4. The product and quotient laws
sections.body_md:
For positive $m$ and $n$ and a valid base $a$:

- **Product law:** $\log_{a}(mn) = \log_{a} m + \log_{a} n$.
- **Quotient law:** $\log_{a}\dfrac{m}{n} = \log_{a} m - \log_{a} n$.

They are the laws of indices $a^{x} a^{y} = a^{x+y}$ and $\dfrac{a^{x}}{a^{y}} = a^{x-y}$ in logarithmic form. Both sides must use the **same base**. A logarithm of a sum or difference does not split: $\log (m + n) \ne \log m + \log n$, and $\dfrac{\log m}{\log n} \ne \log m - \log n$.

Examples: $\log 5 + \log 2000 = \log 10000 = 4$; $\log_{2} 40 - \log_{2} 5 = \log_{2} 8 = 3$.

key_terms.definition_md: The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.
The logarithm of a quotient is the difference of the logarithms.

Log five plus log seven is one point five four four one, the logarithm of thirty five.

sections.heading: 5. The power law
sections.body_md:
**Power law:** $\log_{a} m^{p} = p\log_{a} m$, from $(a^{x})^{p} = a^{px}$. It works for fractions and roots too: $\log \dfrac{1}{8} = -3\log 2$ and $\log \sqrt{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}\log 10 = \dfrac{1}{2}$. In particular $\log_{a} a^{x} = x$.

When a logarithm has a multiplier in front, use the power law first to move it inside: $2\log 5 + 3\log 2 = \log 25 + \log 8 = \log 200$. Check: $4\log 3 - 2\log 9 = \log 81 - \log 81 = \log 1 = 0$.

sections.heading: 6. Expanding and combining; in terms of log 2, log 3, log 5
sections.body_md:
**Expanding:** split products and quotients, then bring the powers down. $\log \dfrac{x^{3} y^{2}}{z} = 3\log x + 2\log y - \log z$. A minus sign in front of a bracket changes every term inside it: $-(\log c^{2} + \log d) = -2\log c - \log d$.

**Combining:** the reverse; powers first, then products and quotients: $2\log 3 + \dfrac{1}{2}\log 16 - \log 6 = \log \dfrac{9 \times 4}{6} = \log 6$.

**In terms of $\log 2$, $\log 3$, $\log 5$:** factorise into $2$, $3$, $5$ and use $\log 10 = 1$, so $\log 5 = 1 - \log 2$: $\log 12 = 2\log 2 + \log 3$ and $\log 0.3 = \log 3 - 1$. With given values: $\log 54 = \log 2 + 3\log 3 = 0.3010 + 1.4313 = 1.7323$.

sections.heading: 7. Equations and identities
sections.body_md:
**Equations.** Combine the logarithms with the laws into one logarithm on each side, convert to exponential form (or equate the arguments), solve, and then **check the domain**: every argument must be positive. A root that makes an argument zero or negative is rejected.

- $\log_{4}(3x - 5) = 2 \Rightarrow 3x - 5 = 16 \Rightarrow x = 7$.
- $\log_{2} x + \log_{2}(x - 2) = 3 \Rightarrow x(x - 2) = 8 \Rightarrow x = 4$ or $-2$; the domain $x > 2$ rejects $-2$.

**Identities.** Start from the more complicated side and use the laws until you reach the other side: $\log 48 - \log 3 = \log 16 = 4\log 2$. If $\log (x + y) = \log x + \log y$ then $x + y = xy$.

key_terms.definition_md: A solution of the algebra that makes an argument non-positive, and so is not a solution of the logarithm equation.

visual.alt: Table of five steps solving log base two of x plus log base two of x minus two equals three. The product law gives x times x minus two equals eight, so x squared minus two x minus eight is zero, so x is four or minus two. Both logarithms need x greater than two, so reject minus two and keep four. Check: two plus one is three.
visual.caption: Always test each root against the domain.

visuals.alt: Table of three steps solving log base four of three x minus five equals two. Write three x minus five equals sixteen, so x is seven. Check the domain: three times seven minus five is sixteen, which is positive.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Conversion between forms (1 mark each):* base, exponent and number in the right places.
- *Evaluate or find an unknown base or number (2 marks):* exponential form 1; result 1 (reject a negative base).
- *Expand or combine (2 marks):* law named and used 1; result 1.
- *Given values (3 marks):* factorise into the given primes 1; laws 1; arithmetic 1.
- *Equation (3 marks):* combine and convert 1; solve 1; domain check 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Swapping $N$ and $x$ when changing form, or forgetting that the base must be positive.
2. Believing $\log_{a} 1 = 1$ or $\log_{a} a = 0$ (it is the other way round).
3. Writing $\log (m + n) = \log m + \log n$, or $\dfrac{\log m}{\log n} = \log m - \log n$.
4. Forgetting that a minus sign in front of a bracket changes every term inside it.
5. Mixing bases in one law.
6. Keeping a root that makes an argument negative; always check the domain.

questions.stem_md: Imran's notebook records the fact $4^{3} = 64$. Which line is the same fact in logarithmic form?
questions.solution_md: In $a^{x} = N$ the base is $a$, the exponent is $x$ and the number is $N$; the logarithmic form is $\log_{a} N = x$. Here $a = 4$, $x = 3$, $N = 64$, so the line is $\log_{4} 64 = 3$. The others swap the base, the exponent and the number.

questions.stem_md: Savita wants $\log_{b} 49 = 2$ to hold for a base $b$ that is positive and not $1$. What must $b$ be?
questions.solution_md: Converting, $b^{2} = 49$, so $b = 7$ or $b = -7$. A base must be positive, so $b = 7$. Check: $7^{2} = 49$.

questions.stem_md: A patch of imagined moss covers $3^{t}$ square centimetres after $t$ weeks. After how many weeks does it cover $243$ square centimetres?
questions.solution_md: We need $3^{t} = 243$. In logarithmic form $t = \log_{3} 243$. Since $3^{5} = 243$, $t = 5$ weeks.

questions.stem_md: An imagined signal meter shows the number $\log_{2} r$ on its dial, where $r$ is the ratio of the signal to the weakest signal. What does the dial show when $r = \dfrac{1}{64}$?
questions.solution_md: We need $x$ with $2^{x} = \dfrac{1}{64}$. Since $64 = 2^{6}$, $\dfrac{1}{64} = 2^{-6}$, so $x = -6$. The dial reads $-6$.

questions.stem_md: Which one of these expressions has no real value?
questions.solution_md: $\log_{5} 0 = x$ would mean $5^{x} = 0$, but a positive base raised to any real power is positive, so no $x$ exists. The other three are fine: $\log_{5} 1 = 0$, $\log_{\frac{1}{2}} 8 = -3$ and $\log_{10} 0.001 = -3$.

questions.stem_md: For every valid base $a$ (that is, $a > 0$ and $a \ne 1$), the value of $\log_{a} a$ is
questions.solution_md: $\log_{a} a = x$ means $a^{x} = a = a^{1}$, so $x = 1$ whatever the base. (It is $\log_{a} 1$ that equals $0$.)

questions.stem_md: A dilute solution has concentration $0.0001$ mole per litre. The common logarithm of this number is
questions.solution_md: Common logarithms use base $10$. $0.0001 = \dfrac{1}{10^{4}} = 10^{-4}$, so $\log 0.0001 = -4$.

questions.stem_md: In the equation $\log_{x} 0.04 = -2$, the base $x$ is
questions.solution_md: In exponential form $x^{-2} = 0.04 = \dfrac{1}{25}$, so $x^{2} = 25$ and $x = 5$ or $-5$. The base must be positive, so $x = 5$. Check: $5^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{25}$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is the product law of logarithms (for positive $m$ and $n$, in any valid base)?
questions.solution_md: Multiplying inside a logarithm corresponds to adding outside: $\log (mn) = \log m + \log n$. For example $\log 6 = \log 2 + \log 3$. The other lines fail at once for $m = 2$, $n = 3$: $\log 2 \times \log 3 \approx 0.144$ is not $\log 6 \approx 0.778$.

questions.stem_md: Rohan combines the two readings $\log 45$ and $\log 9$ by working out $\log 45 - \log 9$. He should write the result as the single logarithm
questions.solution_md: The quotient law gives $\log 45 - \log 9 = \log \dfrac{45}{9} = \log 5$. A difference of logarithms is the logarithm of a quotient, not of a difference ($\log 36$) or of a product ($\log 405$).

questions.stem_md: A dial shows the number $\log_{12}\left(12^{0.4}\right) + \log_{12} 1$. What does it show?
If $\log 2 = p$ and $\log 3 = q$, then $\log 72$ can be written as
questions.solution_md: $72 = 8 \times 9 = 2^{3} \times 3^{2}$, so $\log 72 = 3\log 2 + 2\log 3 = 3p + 2q$. The powers become multipliers, and the product becomes a sum.

questions.stem_md: Meena adds the two readings $\log 5$ and $\log 2000$ on her gauge. The sum is
questions.solution_md: By the product law $\log 5 + \log 2000 = \log (5 \times 2000) = \log 10000$. Since $10000 = 10^{4}$, the sum is $4$.

questions.stem_md: The expression $4\log 3 - 2\log 9$ simplifies to
questions.solution_md: $4\log 3 = \log 3^{4} = \log 81$ and $2\log 9 = \log 9^{2} = \log 81$. Their difference is $\log 81 - \log 81 = \log 1 = 0$.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\log_{2} 40 - \log_{2} 5$ is
questions.solution_md: The quotient law holds in any base: $\log_{2} 40 - \log_{2} 5 = \log_{2} \dfrac{40}{5} = \log_{2} 8 = 3$, because $2^{3} = 8$.

questions.stem_md: For positive $x$, $y$ and $z$, the expression $\log \dfrac{x^{3} y^{2}}{z}$ expands to
questions.solution_md: Product law: $\log (x^{3} y^{2}) = \log x^{3} + \log y^{2}$; quotient law: subtract $\log z$; power law: $\log x^{3} = 3\log x$ and $\log y^{2} = 2\log y$. So the expansion is $3\log x + 2\log y - \log z$.

questions.stem_md: The expression $\log_{5}(x - 4) + \log_{5}(x + 2)$ has a real value only when
questions.solution_md: Each logarithm needs a positive argument: $x - 4 > 0$ gives $x > 4$ and $x + 2 > 0$ gives $x > -2$. Both must hold, and $x > 4$ makes both true. (A value such as $x = -3$ makes both arguments negative and a value such as $x = 0$ makes $x - 4$ negative.)

questions.stem_md: The equation $\log_{2} x + \log_{2}(x - 6) = 4$ is solved by
questions.solution_md: The product law gives $\log_{2}\,x(x - 6) = 4$, so $x(x - 6) = 2^{4} = 16$ and $x^{2} - 6x - 16 = 0$, i.e. $(x - 8)(x + 2) = 0$. Both logarithms need $x > 6$, so $x = -2$ is rejected and $x = 8$ remains. Check: $\log_{2} 8 + \log_{2} 2 = 3 + 1 = 4$.

questions.stem_md:
Kavya finds $\log 360$ from the given values $\log 2 = 0.3010$ and $\log 5 = 0.6990$. Her lines are:

Line 1: $\log 360 = \log (8 \times 45)$.

Line 2: $= \log 8 + \log 45$.

Line 3: $= 3\log 2 + 2\log 5$.

Line 4: $= 3(0.3010) + 2(0.6990) = 2.301$.

questions.stem_md: Since $14 = 7 \times 2$, it follows that $\log 14 = \log 7 \times \log 2$.
questions.solution_md: The product law turns a product into a sum: $\log 14 = \log 7 + \log 2 \approx 0.845 + 0.301 = 1.146$. The product $\log 7 \times \log 2 \approx 0.254$ is quite different.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\log_{b} 1$ is $0$ whichever valid base $b$ is used.
questions.solution_md: $\log_{b} 1 = x$ means $b^{x} = 1$, and $b^{0} = 1$ for every positive $b$, so $x = 0$ for every valid base.

questions.stem_md: The base $x$ of a logarithm satisfies $\log_{x} 343 = \dfrac{3}{2}$. Find $x$.
questions.solution_md: In exponential form $x^{\frac{3}{2}} = 343 = 7^{3}$. Raising both sides to the power $\dfrac{2}{3}$ gives $x = 7^{2} = 49$. Check: $49^{\frac{3}{2}} = 7^{3} = 343$.

questions.stem_md: An imagined algae film covers $3$ square centimetres at noon on day $0$ and its area doubles every day, so after $n$ days it covers $3 \times 2^{n}$ square centimetres. Using $\log 2 = 0.3010$ and $\log 3 = 0.4771$, find the least whole number of days after which the area exceeds $2000$ square centimetres.
questions.solution_md: We need $3 \times 2^{n} > 2000$, so $2^{n} > \dfrac{2000}{3}$. Taking logarithms, $n \log 2 > \log 2000 - \log 3 = 3.3010 - 0.4771 = 2.8239$. Then $n > \dfrac{2.8239}{0.3010} = 9.38\ldots$, so the least whole number is $n = 10$. Check: $3 \times 2^{9} = 1536 < 2000 < 3072 = 3 \times 2^{10}$.

marking_scheme.step: Set up 3 times 2^n greater than 2000 and take logarithms: n log 2 greater than log 2000 minus log 3

questions.solution_md: The quotient law gives $\log_{2}\dfrac{3x - 2}{x - 1} = 2$, so $\dfrac{3x - 2}{x - 1} = 2^{2} = 4$. Then $3x - 2 = 4x - 4$, so $x = 2$. Domain: $3x - 2 = 4 > 0$ and $x - 1 = 1 > 0$, so $x = 2$ is valid. Check: $\log_{2} 4 - \log_{2} 1 = 2 - 0 = 2$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\log 6 + \log 35 - \log 21 = \log \dfrac{6 \times 35}{21} = \log 10 = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Product law for the sum, quotient law for the difference: $\dfrac{6 \times 35}{21} = \dfrac{210}{21} = 10$, and $\log 10 = 1$.

questions.stem_md: Expand $\log \dfrac{p^{5}\sqrt{q}}{r^{3}}$ in terms of $\log p$, $\log q$ and $\log r$, where $p$, $q$, $r$ are positive.

answer.model_answer_md: $\log \dfrac{p^{5}\sqrt{q}}{r^{3}} = \log p^{5} + \log q^{\frac{1}{2}} - \log r^{3} = 5\log p + \dfrac{1}{2}\log q - 3\log r$.

questions.stem_md: Write $2\log 3 + \dfrac{1}{2}\log 16 - \log 6$ as a single logarithm.

answer.model_answer_md: $2\log 3 = \log 9$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}\log 16 = \log 16^{\frac{1}{2}} = \log 4$. So the expression is $\log \dfrac{9 \times 4}{6} = \log 6$.

questions.solution_md: Power law first: $\log 9 + \log 4 - \log 6$. Then product and quotient: $\log \dfrac{36}{6} = \log 6$.

questions.stem_md: For which values of $x$ is the expression $\log_{4}(x - 3) + \log_{4}(10 - x)$ defined?

answer.model_answer_md: Both arguments must be positive: $x - 3 > 0$ gives $x > 3$, and $10 - x > 0$ gives $x < 10$. So the expression is defined for $3 < x < 10$.

questions.solution_md: A logarithm needs a positive argument, so the two conditions $x > 3$ and $x < 10$ must hold together.

questions.stem_md: Solve $\log_{6}(x + 2) + \log_{6}(x - 3) = 1$ and state clearly why any value you reject is rejected.

answer.model_answer_md: $\log_{6}(x + 2)(x - 3) = 1$, so $(x + 2)(x - 3) = 6$. Then $x^{2} - x - 6 = 6$, so $x^{2} - x - 12 = 0$ and $(x - 4)(x + 3) = 0$. Since $x - 3 > 0$ is needed, $x > 3$: $x = -3$ is rejected because $x + 2 = -1$ and $x - 3 = -6$ are negative, and $x = 4$ is accepted.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\log \dfrac{a}{b} + \log \dfrac{b}{c} + \log \dfrac{c}{a} = 0$ for positive $a$, $b$ and $c$.

answer.model_answer_md: By the product law, $\log \dfrac{a}{b} + \log \dfrac{b}{c} + \log \dfrac{c}{a} = \log \left(\dfrac{a}{b} \times \dfrac{b}{c} \times \dfrac{c}{a}\right)$. The product of the three fractions is $\dfrac{abc}{abc} = 1$, so the sum is $\log 1 = 0$.

questions.solution_md: The factors $a$, $b$, $c$ cancel in pairs, leaving $1$; and $\log 1 = 0$ in every base.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Work out $125^{\frac{1}{3}}$ and use it to check that $125^{\frac{2}{3}} = 25$; then write this fact in logarithmic form. [3]

(b) Find the value of $\log_{\frac{1}{4}} 32$. [3]

(c) Find the base $x$ if $\log_{x} 0.001 = -3$, and hence evaluate $\log_{x} x^{5} + \log_{x} 1$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $125^{\frac{1}{3}} = 5$ because $5^{3} = 125$. Then $125^{\frac{2}{3}} = 5^{2} = 25$, so the fact is true. In logarithmic form, $\log_{125} 25 = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

(b) Let $\log_{\frac{1}{4}} 32 = y$. Then $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{y} = 32$, that is $2^{-2y} = 2^{5}$. So $-2y = 5$ and $y = -\dfrac{5}{2}$.

(c) $x^{-3} = 0.001 = \dfrac{1}{1000}$, so $x^{3} = 1000$ and $x = 10$ (a base is positive). Then $\log_{10} 10^{5} = 5$ and $\log_{10} 1 = 0$, so the value is $5 + 0 = 5$.

questions.solution_md: Convert each statement between $a^{x} = N$ and $\log_{a} N = x$, and write both sides over a common prime base when the base is a fraction.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Let $\log_{a} m = x$ and $\log_{a} n = y$. Prove that $\log_{a}(mn) = x + y$. [3]

(b) Prove that $\log_{a} m^{p} = p\log_{a} m$. [3]

(c) Use the laws to evaluate $\log_{2} 3 + \log_{2} 20 - \log_{2} 15 + 2\log_{2} 6 - \log_{2} 9$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) By definition $m = a^{x}$ and $n = a^{y}$. Then $mn = a^{x} \times a^{y} = a^{x + y}$, so in logarithmic form $\log_{a}(mn) = x + y = \log_{a} m + \log_{a} n$.

(b) With $m = a^{x}$, $m^{p} = \left(a^{x}\right)^{p} = a^{px}$, so $\log_{a} m^{p} = px = p\log_{a} m$.

(c) $\log_{2} 3 + \log_{2} 20 - \log_{2} 15 = \log_{2}\dfrac{3 \times 20}{15} = \log_{2} 4 = 2$. Next $2\log_{2} 6 - \log_{2} 9 = \log_{2} 36 - \log_{2} 9 = \log_{2} \dfrac{36}{9} = \log_{2} 4 = 2$. The whole expression is $2 + 2 = 4$.

questions.solution_md: The two proofs turn the laws of indices into laws of logarithms: $a^{x} a^{y} = a^{x + y}$ and $(a^{x})^{p} = a^{px}$. Part (c) applies the product, quotient and power laws.

marking_scheme.step: (c) 2 log_2 6 = log_2 36 and the quotient with 9 gives log_2 4 = 2

questions.stem_md:
An imagined sound meter scores a sound as $S = 10\log\dfrac{I}{I_{0}}$, where $I$ is its intensity and $I_{0}$ is a fixed reference intensity. Use $\log 2 = 0.3010$.

(a) A sound is $4000$ times as intense as the reference. Find its score. [3]

(b) Another sound scores $53.01$. Find the ratio $\dfrac{I}{I_{0}}$. [3]

(c) Show that doubling the intensity of any sound raises its score by $3.01$, whatever the starting intensity. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\dfrac{I}{I_{0}} = 4000 = 4 \times 10^{3}$, so $\log 4000 = 2\log 2 + 3 = 0.6020 + 3 = 3.6020$. Then $S = 10 \times 3.6020 = 36.02$.

(b) $10\log\dfrac{I}{I_{0}} = 53.01$, so $\log\dfrac{I}{I_{0}} = 5.301 = 5 + 0.3010 = \log 10^{5} + \log 2 = \log (2 \times 10^{5})$. Hence $\dfrac{I}{I_{0}} = 200000$.

(c) Let the original score be $S_{1} = 10\log\dfrac{I}{I_{0}}$. Doubling the intensity gives $S_{2} = 10\log\dfrac{2I}{I_{0}} = 10\left(\log 2 + \log\dfrac{I}{I_{0}}\right)$ by the product law. So $S_{2} - S_{1} = 10\log 2 = 10 \times 0.3010 = 3.01$, which does not depend on $I$.

questions.solution_md: Parts (a) and (b) use the product law with powers of ten; part (c) shows that multiplying the intensity adds a fixed amount, $10\log 2$, to the score.

questions.stem_md:
Solve each equation, checking that every logarithm in it is defined for your answer.

(a) $\log_{5}(3x - 2) = 2$ [3]

(b) $\log_{3}(x + 7) - \log_{3}(x - 1) = 2$ [3]

(c) $\log_{3} x + \log_{3}(x + 6) = 3$ [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In exponential form $3x - 2 = 5^{2} = 25$, so $3x = 27$ and $x = 9$. Then $3x - 2 = 25 > 0$, so the logarithm is defined.

(b) The quotient law gives $\log_{3}\dfrac{x + 7}{x - 1} = 2$, so $\dfrac{x + 7}{x - 1} = 9$. Then $x + 7 = 9x - 9$, so $16 = 8x$ and $x = 2$. Both arguments, $9$ and $1$, are positive. Check: $\log_{3} 9 - \log_{3} 1 = 2 - 0 = 2$.

(c) $\log_{3}\,x(x + 6) = 3$, so $x(x + 6) = 27$ and $x^{2} + 6x - 27 = 0$, that is $(x + 9)(x - 3) = 0$. We need $x > 0$, so $x = -9$ is rejected (its logarithms are not defined) and $x = 3$. Check: $\log_{3} 3 + \log_{3} 9 = 1 + 2 = 3$.

(c) reject -9 because x must be positive

questions.stem_md:
(a) Show that $2\log 6 - \log 9 = \log 4$. [3]

(b) Show that $\log\dfrac{9}{10} + \log\dfrac{25}{27} + \log\dfrac{6}{5} = 0$. [3]

(c) The positive numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy $\log (x + y) = \log x + \log y$. Show that $y = \dfrac{x}{x - 1}$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $2\log 6 = \log 6^{2} = \log 36$, so $2\log 6 - \log 9 = \log \dfrac{36}{9} = \log 4$.

(b) By the product law the left side is $\log\left(\dfrac{9}{10} \times \dfrac{25}{27} \times \dfrac{6}{5}\right)$. The product is $\dfrac{9 \times 25 \times 6}{10 \times 27 \times 5} = \dfrac{1350}{1350} = 1$, so the left side is $\log 1 = 0$.

(c) The product law gives $\log x + \log y = \log (xy)$, so $\log (x + y) = \log (xy)$ and therefore $x + y = xy$. Then $xy - y = x$, so $y(x - 1) = x$ and $y = \dfrac{x}{x - 1}$ (with $x \ne 1$; in fact $x > 1$ because $y > 0$).

questions.solution_md: Parts (a) and (b) use the power, product and quotient laws and the fact $\log 1 = 0$. In part (c) two logarithms of the same base are equal only when their arguments are equal.

marking_scheme.step: (c) log(x + y) = log(xy), so x + y = xy

questions.stem_md:
Two imagined rumours spread through a town. Rumour A starts with $5$ people and the number who know it doubles every hour, so after $n$ hours it is $5 \times 2^{n}$. Rumour B starts with $4$ people and triples every hour, so after $m$ hours it is $4 \times 3^{m}$. Use $\log 2 = 0.3010$ and $\log 3 = 0.4771$.

(a) Find the least whole number of hours after which rumour A is known by more than $4000$ people. [3]

(b) Find the least whole number of hours after which rumour B is known by more than $4000$ people. [3]

(c) Which rumour passes $4000$ people first, and by how many whole hours? Support your answer with the number of people who know each rumour after $7$ hours. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $5 \times 2^{n} > 4000$ gives $2^{n} > 800$. Then $n\log 2 > \log 800 = 3\log 2 + 2 = 2.9030$, so $n > \dfrac{2.9030}{0.3010} = 9.64\ldots$. The least whole number is $n = 10$.

(b) $4 \times 3^{m} > 4000$ gives $3^{m} > 1000$. Then $m\log 3 > 3$, so $m > \dfrac{3}{0.4771} = 6.28\ldots$. The least whole number is $m = 7$.

(c) After $7$ hours rumour A is known by $5 \times 2^{7} = 640$ people and rumour B by $4 \times 3^{7} = 8748$ people. Rumour B passes $4000$ after $7$ hours and rumour A only after $10$ hours, so rumour B is first, by $10 - 7 = 3$ hours.

questions.solution_md: Each part turns a growth inequality into $n\log b > \ldots$ by taking logarithms, then rounds up to a whole number of hours.
